claims.claim: Evagrius Ponticus was born in 345 or 346 in Ibora, Pontus, and died in 399 in Cellia, Nitrian Desert, Egypt.

Evagrius was ordained as a lector by Basil of Caesarea and later served as a deacon and archdeacon under Gregory of Nazianzus in Constantinople, where he participated in the Second Ecumenical Council in 381.

Evagrius left his promising ecclesiastical career in 381 or around 382 and traveled to Jerusalem, where he became a monk in 383 in the monastic communities of Rufinus and Melania the Elder, before moving to Egypt.
In Egypt, Evagrius spent the rest of his life in Nitria and Kellia as a monk, spiritual teacher, and writer, supporting himself by copying manuscripts.

The Scholia on Proverbs consists of approximately 382 brief exegetical notes (scholia) on selected passages from the biblical book of Proverbs, rather than a continuous commentary covering the entire book.
Evagrius advised disciples who were just beginning their spiritual journeys to meditate especially on Proverbs, giving the Scholia a foundational position in his community.
A related collection of 28 sentences glossing words found in Proverbs survives in Syriac and Greek in manuscripts including Monacensis gr. 230 (13th century) and Ambrosianus C 69 sup. (16th century).

Evagrius's exegesis in the Scholia is almost exclusively spiritual and symbolic, interpreting Proverbs through three levels of meaning: ethical (practical), physical, and theological, corresponding to the three books of Solomon—Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, and Song of Songs.
The Scholia on Proverbs presents many details about Evagrius's social history and its relation to his theology and his theory of spirituality.
Evagrius's teachings were condemned after his death, though the Armenian and Syrian churches continued to cherish his writings.
